subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Where food comes from and sustainability
Factors affecting food choice and labelling

questions.q: What does the term 'food miles' mean?
options: The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
The number of ingredients in a processed food
The shelf life of a food in days
The energy in kilocalories a food provides
questions.explain: Food miles measure the distance food is transported from producer to consumer, a factor in its environmental impact.

questions.q: Why does buying seasonal, locally grown food generally reduce environmental impact?
options: It requires less transport and heated growing, lowering carbon emissions
It always contains fewer calories
It removes the need for any packaging
It guarantees the food is organic
questions.explain: Local, in-season produce travels shorter distances and needs no artificially heated greenhouses, cutting its carbon footprint.

questions.q: The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) logo on fish products indicates that the fish is:
options: From a certified sustainable, well-managed fishery
Farmed rather than wild-caught
Free from all additives
Suitable for a vegetarian diet
questions.explain: The MSC blue label certifies fish caught from sustainable stocks using responsible methods.

questions.q: What is meant by 'organic' food production?
options: Food grown without most artificial pesticides and fertilisers
Food that contains no carbon
Food grown only in greenhouses
Food that has been genetically modified
questions.explain: Organic farming restricts the use of artificial pesticides, fertilisers and routine antibiotics.

questions.q: The Fairtrade mark on a product mainly signals that:
options: Producers in developing countries received a fair, stable price for their goods
The product is lower in fat than rivals
The food was grown within the UK
No preservatives were used
questions.explain: Fairtrade aims to secure better prices and working conditions for farmers and workers in developing countries.

questions.q: 'Food security' is best described as:
options: All people having reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food
Locking food away to prevent theft
The legal labelling of allergens
The speed at which food is transported
questions.explain: Food security means people can consistently obtain enough safe, nutritious food to stay healthy.

questions.q: A shopper wants to reduce the carbon footprint of their weekly shop. Which choice best achieves this?
options: Buying UK-grown strawberries in summer instead of air-freighted ones in winter
Buying strawberries flown in from abroad out of season
Choosing individually plastic-wrapped imported fruit
Selecting the food with the most food miles
questions.explain: In-season UK produce avoids high-emission air freight and heated growing, lowering the carbon footprint.

questions.q: Turning wheat grain into flour is an example of which type of processing?
options: Primary processing
Secondary processing
Fortification
Preservation
questions.explain: Primary processing converts a raw commodity such as wheat into an ingredient like flour; making bread from flour is secondary processing.

questions.q: By UK law, white and brown flour must be fortified with iron, thiamin, niacin and which other nutrient?
options: Calcium
Vitamin C
Vitamin D
Potassium
questions.explain: UK legislation requires non-wholemeal flour to be fortified with calcium, iron, thiamin (B1) and niacin (B3).

questions.q: Pasteurisation of milk involves:
options: Heating to around 72°C for 15 seconds then rapidly cooling
Freezing to below -18°C
Adding acid to curdle the milk
Removing all the fat
questions.explain: The high-temperature short-time method heats milk to about 72°C for 15 seconds to kill pathogens, then cools it quickly.

questions.q: An emulsifier is added to a food product mainly to:
options: Help oil and water mix and stay combined
Prevent the growth of bacteria
Add an artificial colour
Increase the vitamin content
questions.explain: Emulsifiers stabilise mixtures of oil and water, for example keeping mayonnaise from separating.

questions.q: Why are antioxidants such as vitamin C sometimes added to foods during processing?
options: To slow down oxidation that causes fats to go rancid and cut fruit to brown
To sweeten the product
To make the food thicker
To increase its salt content
questions.explain: Antioxidants delay oxidation reactions, preventing fats turning rancid and stopping enzymic browning.

questions.q: A manufacturer wants a jam to keep for many months without refrigeration. Which processing principle mainly achieves this?
options: A high sugar concentration that limits the water available to microbes
Adding an emulsifier to bind oil and water
Homogenising the fruit into tiny droplets
Fortifying it with iron and calcium
questions.explain: High sugar levels reduce water activity, preserving the jam by preventing microbial growth.

questions.q: Homogenisation of milk is carried out to:
options: Break up fat globules so the cream does not separate to the top
Sterilise the milk completely
Add extra calcium
Ferment the milk into yoghurt
questions.explain: Homogenisation forces milk through fine nozzles to break fat globules into tiny, evenly dispersed droplets.

questions.q: How many named allergens must be emphasised on UK pre-packed food labels?
questions.explain: UK law requires 14 specified allergens, such as milk, eggs, peanuts and gluten-containing cereals, to be highlighted.

questions.q: On a front-of-pack traffic light label, a red colour for saturated fat tells the shopper that the food is:
options: High in saturated fat per portion or 100g
Free from saturated fat
Low in saturated fat
Suitable for vegetarians
questions.explain: Red means high, amber medium and green low, helping consumers compare products at a glance.

questions.q: Which of the following is a legal requirement on a pre-packed food label in the UK?
options: The name of the food and a list of ingredients
The recipe used to develop it
The name of the head chef
The number of food miles travelled
questions.explain: Mandatory label information includes the food's name, ingredients, allergens, weight, use-by/best-before date and storage.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an ethical factor affecting food choice?
options: Choosing free-range eggs because of concern for animal welfare
Choosing a food because it is on special offer
Disliking the taste of a food
Being allergic to peanuts
questions.explain: Ethical choices are based on moral concerns such as animal welfare, fair trade or the environment rather than cost or taste.

questions.q: Meat prepared according to Islamic dietary law is described as:
options: Halal
Kosher
Organic
Vegan
questions.explain: Halal food is permitted under Islamic law; kosher refers to food prepared according to Jewish dietary rules.

questions.q: A customer with coeliac disease is choosing a ready meal. Which label information is most important for them to check?
options: Whether cereals containing gluten are listed among the allergens
The number of food miles travelled
Whether the packaging is recyclable
The Fairtrade certification
questions.explain: People with coeliac disease must avoid gluten, so emphasised gluten-containing cereal allergens are the key information.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Food Preparation & Nutrition (J309) specification; Food Provenance and Food Choice
